drills.title: Advice, collocations and plans
drills.instructions: Type one word in each numbered gap. Use the verb in parentheses where you see one. Then answer questions 5 and 6.

questions.explanation: Take your mind off something means stop thinking or worrying about it for a while.
If I were you introduces advice through an imagined situation.
Use the present simple in the if-clause for a real future possibility.
Make up your mind means make a decision.

questions.prompt: Which action is the teacher actually recommending?
options: Put off all the work until tomorrow.
Ask someone else to choose every example.
Deal with the task that matters most first.
questions.answer: Deal with the task that matters most first.
questions.explanation: She says to start with the most urgent job.

questions.prompt: The writer says, “I put my phone in another room so I could concentrate.” What does the part beginning with so explain?
options: What originally caused the writer to lose focus.
What the writer wanted to achieve.
What happened before the phone was moved.
questions.answer: What the writer wanted to achieve.
questions.explanation: So I could concentrate gives the purpose of moving the phone.

cloze.title: Beating the deadline
cloze.text:
I haven’t been sleeping well, and I’m worried about Friday’s deadline. My teacher suggested taking a short break to take my mind [1] it. She said, ‘[2] I were you, I’d start with the most urgent job.’

If I [3] (sort) out my notes first, I’ll have time to check the final draft tomorrow. I still need to [4] up my mind about which example to leave out.

drills.title: Experiences and imagined choices
drills.instructions: Type one to three words in each numbered gap. Use the words in parentheses where you see them. Then answer questions 5 and 6.

questions.explanation: Use since to give the starting point of an activity that continues into the present.
The first group left before the narrator arrived. Already can also come at the end of the phrase.
Was waiting describes an action already in progress when the guide returned.
The second conditional describes what the speaker would do in an imagined situation.

questions.prompt: Why did the narrator have to wait when they arrived?
options: They had come before the center opened.
They needed to wait for their cousin to finish work.
They had missed the start of the first tour.
questions.answer: They had missed the start of the first tour.
questions.explanation: The first group was already on the trail when the narrator got there.

questions.prompt: “The guide pointed out two rare birds near the lake. They disappeared before I could take a photo.” What does they refer to?
options: The guide and the visitors.
The two rare birds.
The photographs the narrator had planned to take.
questions.explanation: They points back to the two rare birds mentioned in the previous sentence.

cloze.title: A visit to the wildlife center
cloze.text:
My cousin has been working at the wildlife center [1] last May. I went to see her yesterday. By the time I arrived, the first group [2] (already / leave) for the trail, so I had to wait for the next tour.

I was still [3] (wait) at the desk when the guide came back. She told me about their volunteer sessions. If I lived closer, I [4] (volunteer) there every week.
